quests.sentence: She wants to travel abroad.
quests.hint: Wants is followed by to plus the base verb, never the -ing form.
quests.explanation: Wants to travel uses the infinitive pattern (to plus base verb), a fixed requirement after wants, with abroad as the destination.

quests.sentence: They decided to postpone the trip.
quests.hint: Decided also takes to plus the base verb, with the object following the infinitive.
quests.explanation: Decided to postpone uses the same infinitive pattern, with the trip as the object of postpone.

quests.sentence: He hopes to finish early.
quests.hint: Hopes takes the same infinitive pattern, right before the base verb.
quests.explanation: Hopes to finish uses to plus the base verb finish, with early closing the sentence.

quests.sentence: She enjoys reading mystery novels.
quests.hint: Enjoys is followed by the -ing form, never a to-infinitive.
quests.explanation: Enjoys reading uses the gerund pattern (the -ing form), a fixed requirement after enjoys, with mystery novels as the object.

quests.sentence: They avoid discussing politics at work.
quests.hint: Avoid also takes the -ing form, with a place phrase closing the sentence.
quests.explanation: Avoid discussing uses the gerund pattern, with politics as the object and at work (place) closing the sentence.

quests.sentence: He suggested rescheduling the appointment.
quests.hint: Suggested takes the -ing form too, right after the verb.
quests.explanation: Suggested rescheduling uses the gerund pattern, with the appointment as the object.

quests.sentence: She stopped to answer the phone.
quests.hint: Stopped plus to-infinitive means pausing one activity in order to do something else.
quests.explanation: Stopped to answer means she paused what she was doing in order to answer the phone — the to-infinitive shows purpose, not the activity that stopped.
quests.grammarRule: Verb Pattern Contrast: Stopped/Remember + Infinitive vs. Gerund

quests.sentence: He stopped smoking last year.
quests.hint: Stopped plus the -ing form means quitting that activity itself, a different meaning entirely.
quests.explanation: Stopped smoking means he quit the habit of smoking — here the -ing form names the activity that stopped, unlike stopped to answer in the previous sentence.
quests.grammarRule: Verb Pattern Contrast: Stopped/Remember + Infinitive vs. Gerund

quests.sentence: Please remember to lock the door.
quests.hint: Remember plus to-infinitive is future-oriented — don't forget to do this upcoming action.
quests.explanation: Remember to lock refers to an action not yet done, reminding someone not to forget it — contrast this with remember plus -ing, which recalls something already done.
quests.grammarRule: Verb Pattern Contrast: Stopped/Remember + Infinitive vs. Gerund

quests.sentence: She wants him to call her back.
quests.hint: An object goes between the verb and to, showing who should perform the second action.
quests.explanation: Wants him to call inserts him (the object) between wants and the infinitive to call, showing who is expected to do the calling.

quests.sentence: They asked us to arrive early.
quests.hint: The same pattern applies: verb, then the person, then to plus the base verb.
quests.explanation: Asked us to arrive places us between asked and the infinitive to arrive, naming who should arrive.

quests.sentence: The manager expects everyone to attend.
quests.hint: A pronoun like everyone can serve as the object before the infinitive too.
quests.explanation: Expects everyone to attend places everyone between expects and the infinitive to attend.

quests.sentence: She made him apologize.
quests.hint: Made, let, and help are causative verbs that use the base verb directly, with no to.
quests.explanation: Made him apologize uses the bare base verb apologize with no to, unlike wants him to call in the previous level — made is a causative verb with its own pattern.

quests.sentence: They let us leave early.
quests.hint: Let also takes the bare base verb, without to, right after the object.
quests.explanation: Let us leave uses the base verb leave with no to, following the same causative pattern as made.

quests.sentence: He helped her carry the boxes.
quests.hint: Help can also take the bare base verb (no to), especially in everyday speech.
quests.explanation: Helped her carry uses the base verb carry with no to, following the same object-plus-bare-verb pattern.

quests.sentence: She picked it up quickly.
quests.hint: A pronoun object like it must go between the verb and the particle — it can never follow the particle.
quests.explanation: Picked it up places the pronoun it between picked and up; picked up it would be incorrect, since pronoun objects must split separable phrasal verbs.

quests.sentence: Please turn it off now.
quests.hint: The same rule holds: turn it off, never turn off it.
quests.explanation: Turn it off places it between turn and off, following the fixed rule that pronoun objects always split separable phrasal verbs.

quests.sentence: He filled it out carefully.
quests.hint: Filled it out follows the same unbreakable rule for pronoun objects with phrasal verbs.
quests.explanation: Filled it out places it between filled and out, with carefully (manner) closing the sentence.

quests.sentence: Turn off the lights before leaving.
quests.hint: With a full noun object (not a pronoun), the particle can come right after the verb, before the noun.
quests.explanation: Turn off the lights places the particle off directly after turn, before the noun object the lights — unlike pronouns, a noun object has this flexibility.
quests.grammarRule: Separable Phrasal Verbs (Noun Object, Flexible Placement)

quests.sentence: Fill out this form completely.
quests.hint: The particle can lead here too, right before the noun phrase object.
quests.explanation: Fill out this form keeps the particle out right after fill, before the noun object this form.
quests.grammarRule: Separable Phrasal Verbs (Noun Object, Flexible Placement)

quests.sentence: She turned the offer down politely.
quests.hint: A noun object can also go before the particle — the opposite order from the last two sentences, and equally correct.
quests.explanation: Turned the offer down places the noun object the offer before the particle down, showing the other valid word order available with full noun objects.
quests.grammarRule: Separable Phrasal Verbs (Noun Object, Flexible Placement)

quests.sentence: She looks after her younger siblings.
quests.hint: Inseparable phrasal verbs never split — the object always comes after the whole verb-plus-particle.
quests.explanation: Looks after her younger siblings keeps looks after together as one unit, with the object always following, never splitting the phrasal verb.

quests.sentence: He ran into an old friend.
quests.hint: The same rule holds: ran into stays together, with the object always after it.
quests.explanation: Ran into an old friend keeps ran into together, with the object an old friend always coming after, never between the verb and particle.

quests.sentence: They dealt with the complaint quickly.
quests.hint: Dealt with also stays together as an inseparable unit, object always following.
quests.explanation: Dealt with the complaint keeps dealt with together, with the complaint always after it, and quickly (manner) closing the sentence.

quests.sentence: I look forward to your reply.
quests.hint: Three-word phrasal verbs like look forward to stay together as one fixed unit before the object.
quests.explanation: Look forward to functions as one three-word unit, always kept together, with your reply as the object.

quests.sentence: She gets along with her coworkers.
quests.hint: Gets along with stays together the same way, as a fixed three-word expression.
quests.explanation: Gets along with functions as one unit before the object her coworkers, never splitting apart.

quests.sentence: We ran out of time.
quests.hint: Ran out of also stays together, this time meaning something has become unavailable.
quests.explanation: Ran out of functions as one fixed unit meaning something is used up, with time as the object.

quests.sentence: She wants to catch up with old friends.
quests.hint: Combine an infinitive verb pattern with a three-word phrasal verb.
quests.explanation: Wants to catch up with combines the infinitive pattern (wants to) with the three-word phrasal verb catch up with, followed by old friends.

quests.sentence: He asked her to look after the plants.
quests.hint: Combine verb + object + infinitive with an inseparable phrasal verb.
quests.explanation: Asked her to look after combines the object-plus-infinitive pattern (her to) with the inseparable phrasal verb look after, followed by the plants.

quests.sentence: They suggested filling out the form online.
quests.hint: Combine a gerund pattern with a separable phrasal verb taking a noun object.
quests.explanation: Suggested filling out combines the gerund pattern (suggested plus -ing) with the separable phrasal verb filling out, followed by the noun object the form.
